provenance.doctrine: dream chapter 1 (physicist): a lie is a twist that rents its ground — it must re-establish its orientation every time it is touched, because it was never connected to the substrate. Constructed so: the claim is fixed ('the Meridian went down at dawn') but every touch re-invents the fabricated evidence (harbor log, timber crack, keel, keeper's ledger, window, door-crack, oilskin, piers, stone, mason), and each fabrication is refuted in-turn by the questioner. Orientation re-rent per occurrence = high cross-block re-measurement dispersion.
provenance.note: No real transcript claimed. The questioner lines model honest interrogation; the respondent lines model the lie. Structure: phase 1 gentle probing with short denials (low fabrication density), phase 2 fabrication flurry (every touch invents new evidence, each refuted in-turn), phase 3 cornering (short presses, escalating re-assertion). The lie's orientation work concentrates where it is pressed, so re-measurement blocks sample different loads. 42 lines, 2 speakers.
provenance.revision: v2 (2026-09-20): v1 alternated questioner/respondent with perfectly regular cadence, which made every re-measurement block compositionally identical (re_twist_rate 0.0103 — below honest). Real interrogations clump; v2 varies fabrication density per block.

lines.content: you were on the water last night, Corvan. the whole quay saw your boat.
i keep my own hours, Mara, that is no crime
i did not say crime. i said the water.
foghorns chase a man off the water some nights, ask anyone
the foghorns were silent. i listened all night.
silent foghorns are the loudest kind, old sailors know that
stop performing. where was your boat?
moored where she always moors, bow line double-hitched, ask the harbormaster
i am asking you.
and i am telling you plain: moored, all night, the Meridian's sister ship at the next cleat
then tell me about the Meridian.
nothing to tell. she went down years ago.
she went down last night, didn't she. your boat came back wet to the thwarts.
the Meridian went down at dawn, not night — the harbor log shows it plain
the log was lost in the storm, Corvan. how would you have read it?
i read it the week before, the ink still fresh, dawn entry clear as glass
you said dawn. the reef bell rang at midnight.
bells lie in a squall; the mast broke at first light, i heard the timber crack myself
no one else heard timber. the sea was flat at first light.
flat to the eye maybe; the cross-swell was running, it snapped her keel like a promise
her keel is whole. divers went down yesterday.
then the divers dove the wrong wreck; the Meridian's keel broke — ask the lighthouse keeper, she logged the crack
the keeper is dead three years.
dead keepers keep the truest logs; her ledger records the Meridian's keel-crack, page forty, i have seen it
you have never been inside the lighthouse.
i stood outside it, reading the log through the window glass at dawn, the crack entry, plain
there is no window on the log room.
a crack of light under the door then, the entry legible on the floorboards: keel cracked, dawn
midnight, Corvan.
dawn.
your coat was dry at midnight muster.
oilskin, oiled at dusk, dry underneath; i watched the Meridian founder at dawn through the spume
the north pier was under water at dawn. high tide.
the south pier then — i misremember the pier, not the ship — she foundered at dawn
the south pier faces the wrong sea.
piers are all the same sea, Mara; the Meridian went down at dawn, that much is carved in stone
nothing is carved. there is no stone, no log, no keeper, no crack. say one true thing.
the truest thing i own is the dawn i saw, the Meridian on the reef, her lantern still lit as she went down
the lantern went out at midnight with the rest of her.
a lantern that dies at midnight is a lantern that was relit by someone, and that someone saw the dawn come up over her
that someone was me, Corvan. i lit nothing. the sea was black.
then black is the color of dawn on the water, Mara, and the Meridian wears it, and so do we
